newsitem.title: COMOROS: Civil servants strike in Comoro islands.
newsitem.headline: Civil servants strike in Comoro islands.

text.p: Civil servants on the Comoros islands went on strike on Thursday, shortly after President Mohamed Taki named a new government, to protest against salary arrears of up to a year.
On the island of Anjuan, the civil servants heeded calls by union leaders and took to the streets to protest against the salary delays.
In other parts of the Indian Ocean archipelago, medical services and schools were disrupted after unions declared an indefinite strike.
The unions had given Taki's government until the end of December to pay civil servants their salary arrears or face nation-wide industrial unrest. But the government failed to meet the deadline.
Taki has appointed a new 11-member government under Prime Minister Ahmed Abdou four weeks after general elections in the Indian Ocean archipelago, officials said on Thursday.
They said the new government, the third since Taki was elected president in March, was dominated by newcomers and included only three ministers from the previous 14-member government.

Mouhtar Ahmed Charif, Taki's former cabinet director, was appointed foreign minister, while Mohamed Ali Soilihi, a former high commissioner of planning, was named minister of finance, the budget and economy.

The new government under Abdou, 60, a veteran administrator who has held the finance ministry portfolio several times, takes over public finances which are in a catastrophic state with most civil servants unpaid for the past 11 months.
In a new year address on Wednesday on behalf of the president, Abdou promised to work to restore trust between the government, the Comoran people and multilateral aid donors.
Abdou was appointed prime minister last Friday following elections on December 1 boycotted by the opposition.
Taki's ruling party, the National Rally for Development, won 36 of the 43 seats in the federal assembly. Independents won four and the Islamist party three.
The opposition boycotted the polls, saying it feared they would be rigged. The tiny Indian Ocean island archipelago has had up to 17 coups or attempted coups since independence from France in 1975.
